analysis.one_liner: Phases out the subminimum wage for workers with disabilities and pays employers to move them into regular jobs.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2025 with bipartisan Senate support and referred to the Senate labor committee, the bill has seen no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: A 1938 law allows employers with a special federal certificate to pay workers with disabilities less than the minimum wage. This bill would immediately raise those wages to 60% of the federal minimum, step them up to the full minimum over five years, ban any new certificates, and end the program entirely, while awarding grants to states and employers to help move disabled workers into regular jobs in the community. It authorizes $200 million a year for five years to pay for the transition, plus audits and annual reports on the wages being paid.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers with disabilities who are currently paid under special certificates below the federal minimum wage — the bill guarantees them a rising wage floor ending at full minimum wage, plus help finding and keeping regular community jobs and wraparound support services.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers with disabilities paid subminimum wages

how_it_helps.text: Raises the wage floor for certificate holders to 60% of the federal minimum wage within 90 days of enactment, stepping to 70%, 80%, 90%, and finally the full federal minimum over five years [S2].
Bars the Labor Department from issuing any new special certificates and sunsets the program five years after enactment, ending subminimum pay altogether [S2].

Creates grant programs — $3 million to $15 million per state over five years and $200,000 to $750,000 per employer over three years — to help businesses and nonprofits shift from segregated subminimum work to paying full wages in competitive integrated jobs [S2].

Prioritizes people with the most significant disabilities, including intellectual and developmental disabilities, for employment supports during the transition, and requires an independent multi-year evaluation plus an audit of at least 10% of certificate holders in the first year [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers holding 14(c) certificates — mostly disability service nonprofits running segregated workshops, plus some for-profit contractors — lose the ability to pay reduced wages, though the grants cushion the cost; federal taxpayers fund the $200 million annual authorization.

drawbacks.text: The $200 million a year is only an authorization, not guaranteed money — Congress would have to appropriate it each year, and if it does not, the transition supports the wage mandate depends on could fall short [S2].
The ramp is slow: workers can still legally be paid 60% of the minimum wage for the first two years and 70% for the first three, so many affected workers wait years for full pay [S2].

The bill's own design acknowledges the risk that some workers with the most significant disabilities may struggle to find competitive jobs — it requires they be given priority for employment supports and integrated services, which providers and some families have historically argued may not fully replace the structured setting of a workshop (general knowledge about how 14(c) programs operate).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: a guaranteed wage floor ending legal subminimum pay for a group of workers who have been exempt from it since 1938, against the upheaval of businesses and nonprofits that were built around paying reduced wages. The bill tries to manage that upheaval with a five-year ramp, money for providers to restructure, and support services for the workers themselves. The main weaknesses are the funding — an authorization, not a guarantee — and the slow initial ramp, both of which shift risk onto the very workers the bill is meant to help.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2025, read twice, and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which has taken no further action on it [S4].

narrative.text: Sen. Chris Van Hollen introduced the bill on July 24, 2025, joined as original cosponsors by Sens. Steve Daines, Kirsten Gillibrand, and Marsha Blackburn — a bipartisan four [S2].
Seven senators total cosponsored the bill: 4 of 55 Senate Republicans and 3 of 45 Senate Democrats [S3].
After being read twice, the bill was referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on July 24, 2025, and the record shows no hearing, markup, vote, or further action since [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, the status quo holds: employers holding special certificates continue paying subminimum wages, and no one has had to change anything because the bill has not moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers keeping the subminimum status quo

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship is genuinely split: the bill was introduced by a Democrat with Republican original cosponsors, and its seven cosponsors break down as 4 Republicans and 3 Democrats [S3].

industries.note: These employers lose the legal right to pay workers with disabilities less than minimum wage, but they also receive federal grants of up to $750,000 each to restructure into competitive integrated employment models. Their interest in keeping subminimum wage labor runs against the workers they employ, which is precisely what the bill is designed to end.

For-profit and public-sector customers who buy goods and services produced at subminimum wages (such as laundry, janitorial, and assembly contracts) would pay more as the wage floor rises, but the bill guarantees those disabled workers the same minimum wage as any other employee.

industries.industry: Disability employment and vocational service agencies
industries.note: States and nonprofits specializing in placing people with disabilities into community jobs would receive the transformation grants, technical assistance funding, and supported employment funding the bill creates.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Senate HELP Committee with no scheduled action. Most bills referred to committee in a divided Congress never get a hearing or vote, and this one has drawn only seven cosponsors despite its bipartisan start; unless the committee schedules it or it is attached to a larger package, it is likely to expire without a vote at the end of the 119th Congress.
